extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of philosophy and literary criticism; creative writers interested in imagination, memory, and the theory of perception
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and prescriptive remarks about the imagination, memory, and the conditions of philosophical and poetic thought — what faculties and dispositions enable genuine poetic imagination and reliable memory, and what a satisfactory theory of perception must explain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imagination (intermediate faculty; active & passive)
rubrics_metrics.description: The imagination is an intermediate faculty, at once active and passive, which mediates between the active and passive powers of the mind; in common language, and especially on the subject of poetry, 'imagination' denotes a superior degree of this faculty joined to a superior voluntary control over it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The will can confine and intensify attention to give vividness or distinctness to any object; the mental process of thinking is analogous to alternate active and passive pulses (emblem: a little water-insect ascending a stream). For poetry, aim for a high degree of imaginative faculty combined with voluntary control. Beware schemes that claim to produce artificial memory or fancy—these only produce confusion and debasement of the fancy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arts of Memory (constitutive dispositions and habits)
rubrics_metrics.description: The true 'Arts of Memory' are: sound logic (habitual subordination of the individual to the species and of species to genus); philosophical knowledge of facts in relation of cause and effect; a cheerful and communicative temper; a quiet conscience; freedom from anxieties; sound health; and above all, healthy digestion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These natural dispositions and habits are the best and only reliable arts of memory. Attempts at artificial systems promising mechanical improvement of memory are useless or absurd and tend to debase the imagination.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conditions from causes (avoid sophism)
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not mistake the conditions of a thing for its causes and essence; nor confuse the process by which we learn of a faculty with the faculty itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply this distinction when analyzing philosophical systems (example: the air is a condition of life, not its cause). Contemporary coincidence (Leibnitz's Lex Continui) and contemporaneity are conditions enabling association, but are not themselves causes. Use cross-examination of schemes (e.g., Hartley) to reveal paralogisms that conflate condition with cause.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement for a theory of perception
rubrics_metrics.description: Any adequate theory of association or of the mind must supply (or at least not supplant) a theory of perception and must explain the formation of the 'associable' (the items capable of being associated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Systems such as Dualism, Hylozoism, and Materialism, as commonly taught, fail because they do not explain how the object itself (not merely sensations or impressions) is immediately present to consciousness. A satisfactory philosophical account must address the 'how' of perception, not merely assert correspondences or dream-world analogies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Materialist test: explain transition from external impact to perception
rubrics_metrics.description: A materialist account must show how an affection or impact from without can metamorphose itself into perception or will within the percipient; mere propagation of motion into motion is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critique of crude materialism: motion propagating motion cannot yield an inward subjective perception. If thinking is to be explained materially, matter must be refined into a modification of intelligence with functions of appearing and perceiving; otherwise the account is unintelligible or reduces to an empty ghost of matter. The burden is to make intelligible the presence of the object itself in consciousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prudence in philosophical expression (veracity of intention)
rubrics_metrics.description: Veracity is not merely the literal saying of truths but the intention to communicate truth; philosophers may sometimes need to express themselves mythically or equivocally to avoid harm or persecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When full disclosure would convey falsehoods or excite malignant passions, prudent expression (mythic or equivocal) can be justified. Kant's caution is cited: discretion in exposition can be a methodological virtue when danger or misunderstanding would otherwise ensue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assessment of originality (shared background and coincidence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Similarity of thought or phrase is not conclusive evidence of plagiarism; coincidences can arise from shared intellectual preparation and common study (e.g., Kantian background).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating claims of borrowing, consider common influences, shared schools of thought, and chronological exposure. Give credit for priority where due, but recognize that independent coincidence is possible when authors work from the same preparatory philosophy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Value of simple/mystic writings (judge by spirit and judgement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Writings of humble or unlearned mystics may contain fulness of heart and genuine insight that rival or exceed learned folios; to profit from them the reader must bring spirit and judgment superior to that of the writer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss simple expression as mere delusion; evaluate such works by their heartfelt quality and inward truth rather than by scholastic discipline alone. The critic should be open to inspiration expressed in simple language and avoid condescension toward non-literary sources of insight.
